title: Coral Reefs and the Partnership That Builds Them
subject: eco
paras: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species. This remarkable diversity depends on a partnership between two very different organisms: the coral animal and the single-celled algae that live inside its tissues.

A coral reef is built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp is a soft, tube-shaped creature only a few millimeters across, with a ring of tentacles around its mouth. Polyps extract calcium and carbonate from seawater and use them to build hard limestone skeletons beneath their bodies. As generations of polyps grow on top of the skeletons of their ancestors, the structure slowly rises, sometimes by only a centimeter a year. Large reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef have taken thousands of years to form.

Building limestone requires a great deal of energy, and reef-building corals obtain most of it from algae known as zooxanthellae. The algae live within the polyps' cells and carry out photosynthesis, using sunlight to produce sugars. They pass up to 90 percent of this food to their host. In return, the coral provides the algae with a protected home and with carbon dioxide and nutrients from its own waste. This exchange explains why reef-building corals are found only in shallow, clear water: the algae need light to survive.

The relationship also explains why reefs are vulnerable to rising ocean temperatures. When water becomes even one or two degrees warmer than normal for several weeks, the algae's photosynthesis begins to produce harmful chemicals. The coral responds by expelling the algae. Because the algae give coral much of its color, the coral turns white, a process called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but without its partners it is starving. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can recolonize the coral; if not, the coral may die.

Scientists are now investigating whether some corals can survive warmer conditions. Certain types of algae appear to tolerate heat better than others, and corals that host these types sometimes recover from bleaching more successfully. Some researchers are even breeding heat-resistant corals in laboratories with the goal of planting them on damaged reefs. Whether such efforts can work on a large enough scale remains uncertain, but they show how closely the future of reefs is tied to the partnership at their core.
